title: Medicare Enrollment: 3 mistakes to avoid when aging into Medicare
summary: This article describes the key mistakes people often make when they age into and enroll in Medicare
body_text: Medicare Enrollment: 3 mistakes to avoid when aging into Medicare By Whitney Stidom , Vice President of Consumer Enablement, eHealth More Americans are born during August than any other month , which means more people are aging into Medicare now than at any other point in the year . Across the country, a s many as 11,000 Americans become Medicare-eligible every day. While turning 65 and becoming eligible for Medicare is a major life milestone , 75% of beneficiaries say choosing coverage is confusing. That’s in part because n ew enrollees must quickly understand whether their doctors , pharmacies, hospitals and facilities are in network , how much they might pay out of pocket for medical care and pre scription needs , and the key differences between the various Medicare coverage options . If you or a loved in will soon be celebrating a 65 th birthday and aging into Medicare, avoiding the following three mistakes can help improve access to care, reduce the risk of surprise medical costs , and contribute to overall well-being. Mistake #1: Missing your initial Medicare enrollment window Your initial election period under Medicare typically begins three months before you turn 65, includes your birth month, and extends three months afterward. Missing the i nitial e nrollment p eriod can lead to delayed or denied coverage and financial penalties that last a lifetime . For instance, if you miss the initial enrollment period and then decide to add a Medicare Supplement plan, you can be declined coverage or charged more based on your medical history. If you stick with Original Medicare, enrolling late in Medicare Pa rt B can result in paying lifetime surcharges on your premiums, starting at about $240 more per year (in 2026) and going up from there depending on the length of the delay . Unfortunately, a recent survey of people approaching Medicare age (55 to 64) found most are unaware of these potential penalties. It’s important to m ark key enrollment dates on your calendar before your 65th birthday and underst and w hether your employment status or employer coverage may affect your Medicare enr ollment timeline. Mistake #2: Ignoring prescription drug coverage Some people think Medicare automatically covers prescription drug s , but that is not the case . Other s may incorrectly assume they can sign up for prescription drug coverage when ever they need it, without consequences . The truth is that delaying enrollment in Medicare Par t D drug coverage or letting prescription drug coverage lapse can become more expensive later. Medicare may impose a late-enrollment penalty if you go too long without creditable prescription drug coverage after becoming eligible for Medicare . That penalty continue s for as long as you remain enrolled in a Medicare Part D plan, starting at about $ 56 extra per year (in 2026) for every year you went without Medicare drug coverage . Even if you rarely visit a pharmacy today, prescription needs can change unexpectedly , and the risk of developing chronic conditions increases by age . In fact, 88 % of Americans 65 and older take at least one prescription medication. Evaluating your drug coverage options when you first become eligible may help protect both your health and your future budget. Mistake #3: Mismatching you r Medicare plan with your lifestyle & budget Do you know the difference between Original Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Medicare Supplement, and Part D? If not, you are not alone : Research shows j ust 13% of current Medicare enrollees can correctly identify the definition for all of these . E ducating yourself about your Medicare plan options before you enroll can help you find the best match for your budget and lifestyle. While Original Medicare (Parts A and B) helps pay for hospital and doctor c are, it leaves beneficiaries responsible for out-of-pocket expenses and lacks prescription drug coverage. To fill those gaps , more people are enrolling in Medicare Advantage, which bundles Medicare Part s A and B into a plan offered by a private insurer . Most of these plans include prescription drug coverage and an annual cap on out-of-pocket costs , and many includ e bene fits such as dental, vision, and hearin g care . The other option is a Medicare Supplem ent (M edigap) plan, which works alongside Original Medicare and can reduce out-of-pocket medical expenses . Multiple factors, including your current health statu s, abilit y to pay monthly premi ums , and trav el pla ns , will help determine which coverage option is a better option for you. By better understanding eligible enrollment dates and plan options, turning 65 can be a reason for celebration while providing the opportunity to make the right health pla n coverage decision for you . Whitney Stidom is vice president of consumer enablement at eHealth , an online health insurance marketplace that helps consumers navigate their health benefit decisions

title: Don’t let new software become shelfware
summary: Focus on software adoption to help maximize application value
body_text: Delivering new software to users isn’t the finish line—it’s actually the starting point. Once a solution is successfully deployed many IT teams walk away, believing the job is finished. That’s why projects often stall after go-live; user adoption is left to the users. When users aren’t clear on the goal or benefits of adopting new software, they may resent the way it forces them to change their day-to-day work. This can lead to workarounds or refusal to use it. When that happens, innovative features of the new software are never explored, the promise of business benefits disappear, and return on investment (ROI) becomes a non-starter. The benefits of focusing on user adoption To get the most out of new software, organizations should focus on boosting user adoption to deliver the maximum value of their software investment. Increasing user adoption can help organizations: Accelerate ROI through faster time to value. Reduce IT support tickets with targeted, relevant training. Increase employee productivity and ensure sure key features are taken advantage of to drive business benefits. How to improve user adoption There are a few key elements to a successful user adoption program: Measurable technical indicators – Organizations need these indicators to replace guesswork with meaningful data. Hard facts will help you tie software investments to business outcomes and better predict ROI. And you can drive continuous improvement by tracking the impact the software has on workflows over time. Identification of the No. 1 adoption constraint – You can’t fix the problem if you don’t know where it is. Whether it’s a technical glitch, lack of user training, or misaligned workflow, spotting that one issue standing in the way of adoption most can help you address it quickly. That way you can offer highly targeted training for underused features so users better understand how to take advantage them, which maximizes the software’s benefits. Clear technical and enablement actions – Once gaps are identified, they need to be addressed. Technical actions can help solve adoption issues by ensuring the software is well integrated into established processes, addresses the correct workflow, and upholds organizational standards for security, privacy, compliance, etc. User enablement actions can help build trust, drive changes, and boost proficiency. Alignment of platform capabilities to business outcomes – Regardless of user adoption, if the new software doesn’t deliver the desired business outcomes it won’t be considered a success. Be sure the expected benefits are understood by the business, the IT team, and the users, and that users are specifically trained on how to use the software’s features that drive these results. And ensure the software has access to the necessary data that is clean, governed, and well managed to deliver the desired output. A Success Program Manager – Incorporating a Success Program Manager to support adoption ensures accountability and sustained momentum beyond deployment. This dedicated role bridges the gap between IT and the business by continuously monitoring adoption metrics, aligning stakeholders on desired outcomes, and proactively addressing barriers to usage. By orchestrating communication, tracking progress against KPIs, and driving ongoing optimization of the adoption framework, a Success Program Manager helps ensure the software delivers measurable business value and that adoption becomes a long-term success rather than a one-time effort. Software only delivers value when it’s actually used. Leveraging a structured framework for adoption can turn promised capabilities into measurable impact. By focusing on the right constraints and aligning to outcomes, you ensure every implementation drives real results. Learn more about OpenText™ Client Success Services and the OpenText Solution Adoption Planning Framework.

title: Manual Verification for Non-DOT Employment: How to Close the Gap §391.23 Leaves Open
summary: A CDL applicant's employment history runs 10 years, but §391.23's mandated investigation only reaches DOT-regulated employers from the past 3. Everything else — warehouse jobs, self-employment, years 4 through 10 — must be verified manually. Here's the workflow that produces a defensible DQ file.
body_text: Most DOT compliance content stops at 49 CFR 391.23 — the three-year safety performance history investigation, the 30-day response window, the drug and alcohol testing inquiry. That regulation is well covered, including in our own guide to executing FMCSA-compliant previous employment verification . What gets far less attention is everything §391.23 doesn't reach. A CDL applicant hands you an employment application covering ten years. Some of those employers are DOT-regulated motor carriers. Many are not — a warehouse, a construction outfit, two years driving a delivery van for a florist, eighteen months of self-employment, a gap the applicant describes as "helping with family business." None of that lives in the Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse. None of it shows up in PSP. Most of it isn't in a commercial verification database either. It still has to be verified, and the only way to verify it is to pick up the phone. This is the workflow for that. The Two Clocks Most DQ Files Confuse The single most common source of confusion in driver qualification files is treating "employment history" as one requirement with one lookback period. It's two requirements with two different scopes. Clock one — the application. Under 49 CFR 391.21(b)(11), the employment application must capture the applicant's employment history. For drivers subject to CDL requirements, FMCSA's guidance and the companion notification rule at 49 CFR 383.35 push that history out to ten years of commercial motor vehicle employment. For non-CDL drivers, the application requirement is three years . Clock two — the investigation. Under 49 CFR 391.23, the prospective employer must conduct a safety performance history investigation of the applicant's DOT-regulated employers during the preceding three years . That investigation has specific content requirements: general employment verification, accident history, and — where the applicant held a safety-sensitive position — drug and alcohol testing history. The gap between those two clocks is where files fail. Years four through ten are on the application but outside the §391.23 investigation. Non-DOT employers inside the three-year window are on the application but outside the §391.23 investigation. In both cases the entry is on the form, the auditor can see it, and nothing in the file shows anyone ever confirmed it was true. §391.23 tells you which employers you must investigate under a specific protocol. It does not tell you that the rest of the application can go unverified. What Counts as Non-DOT Employment An employer falls outside §391.23's mandated investigation when the applicant's position there was not a safety-sensitive function for a DOT-regulated entity. In practice, on real applications, this means: Non-transportation jobs entirely — warehouse, retail, food service, construction, manufacturing, landscaping Driving jobs below CDL thresholds — box trucks under 26,001 lbs, delivery vans, courier work for non-regulated employers Employers outside the three-year window — a DOT-regulated carrier the applicant left four years ago is on the ten-year application but outside the §391.23 investigation Self-employment and owner-operator periods where the applicant was not leased to a regulated carrier Gaps — unemployment, education, incarceration, caregiving, military service That last category deserves its own note. A gap is not an absence of information; it is a claim. "Unemployed, March 2023 to January 2024" is an assertion about the applicant's history, and a defensible file documents what you did to test it. Why Databases Can't Touch This The verification tooling built for DOT compliance is scoped to DOT data. That's the point of it, and it's also its limit. The Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse contains violation and testing records for CDL holders in safety-sensitive positions. PSP returns FMCSA crash and inspection data for regulated carriers. Neither system has any record of the eight months an applicant spent on a warehouse floor. Commercial instant-verification databases have a different problem: coverage skew. Their records come from payroll processors and large employer contributions, which means they cover big national employers well and small regional ones poorly. The non-DOT entries on a driver's application are disproportionately small employers — a two-truck landscaping company, a regional food distributor, a family construction business. Those are precisely the records the databases don't hold. The result is that the harder half of a driver's employment history is also the half no automated system will resolve. Someone has to call. The Manual Non-DOT Verification Workflow This is the sequence that produces a file an auditor can follow. It runs in parallel with your §391.23 requests, not after them — waiting for the DOT investigations to close before starting the non-DOT work is how carriers blow their onboarding timelines. 1. Segment the application on intake. Before any outreach, mark every employer entry as DOT-regulated in-window, DOT-regulated out-of-window, non-DOT, self-employment, or gap. Each segment gets a different protocol. Doing this at intake rather than midstream is what keeps the two clocks from blurring. 2. Confirm the employer exists and find the right contact. For small employers this is the actual work. Business registration lookups, the state secretary of state database, and a plain web search will usually establish whether the company is still operating and produce a current number. Record what you searched and what you found, including dead ends. 3. Call, with a specific ask. Non-DOT verification is narrower than a §391.23 inquiry. You are confirming dates of employment, position held, and — where the employer will provide it and your permissible purpose supports it — reason for separation. You are not asking for drug and alcohol testing records, because the employer has no DOT obligation to hold or release them. 4. Escalate through channels, not through repetition. A second and third call to the same unanswered line is not a good-faith effort; it's the same effort three times. Move to email, then to a written request, then to a documented alternate contact. Our guidance on how CRAs handle the long tail of unresponsive employers covers the escalation ladder in detail. 5. Document the negative outcomes too. A verification you could not complete is a fact about the file. "Employer defunct — confirmed dissolved with state registry on 2026-07-14, registry screenshot attached" is a defensible entry. A blank line is not. 6. Reconcile gaps against adjacent employers. When an applicant claims a gap between two jobs, the end date from the prior employer and the start date from the next one should bracket it cleanly. Overlaps and mismatches are the signal worth chasing. What Auditors Actually Look For on Non-DOT Entries FMCSA compliance reviews focus on §391.23 because that's the mandated investigation, and incomplete pre-employment screening is a perennial top finding. But the file gets read as a whole, and reviewers notice patterns. The findings that recur on the non-DOT side: Unexplained blanks. An application entry with no corresponding verification record and no documentation of attempts. Timeline holes. Ten years of required history with fourteen months unaccounted for and nothing in the file acknowledging it. Undated notes. "Called, no answer" without a date, time, number dialed, or the name of the person who called. Verification by applicant. Using a phone number the applicant supplied, reaching someone who confirms everything, and never independently establishing that the number belongs to the employer. That last one is worth dwelling on. A verification is only as good as the independence of the contact path. If the applicant provides the number and the applicant's friend answers it, the file contains a confirmation and no verification. For the broader picture of what reviewers request and how they probe, see what FMCSA audit reviewers look for in CDL employment verification . How Superunit Completes the Non-DOT Long Tail Superunit was built for exactly the segment that databases skip. Our model is that automated outreach handles the sequence — dialing, navigating phone trees, holding, re-attempting across business hours and time zones, escalating to fax and email on schedule — while human specialists handle the exceptions that need judgment. That split matters most on non-DOT entries, because non-DOT employers are where the exceptions concentrate. A two-person landscaping company has no HR department, no verification line, and no process. Getting a real answer out of it means reaching a specific person at a specific hour and asking a question they've never been asked before. Superunit has completed more than 200,000 verifications , and the model was built for this hard segment specifically — the cases that arrive because a database already returned nothing. What Superunit Logs on Every Non-DOT Verification What comes back only matters if it survives a compliance review. Every Superunit verification produces a structured record built for the DQ file rather than for a dashboard: Field What it captures Contact path The number or address used, and how it was independently sourced Attempt log Every attempt with date, time, channel, and outcome Respondent Name and role of the person who provided the information Data returned Dates of employment, position, separation reason where provided Discrepancies Any conflict with the applicant's stated history, flagged Terminal status Verified, refused, defunct, or unreachable — with supporting evidence The distinction that matters at audit is between "we couldn't verify this" and "here is the documented sequence of attempts that establishes we tried in good faith and here is what we found." The second is a defensible file. For how this documentation chain fits the broader qualification file, see building a DOT driver qualification file audit trail . Frequently Asked Questions Is manual verification of non-DOT employment legally required? §391.23's mandated safety performance history investigation applies to DOT-regulated employers in the preceding three years. Non-DOT entries fall outside that specific requirement. However, the application itself must be complete and accurate under §391.21, and carriers carry independent negligent-hiring exposure for unverified history. Most compliance programs verify the full application as a matter of policy. Confirm your own obligations with counsel. How far back should we verify non-DOT employment? Match the application requirement. For CDL applicants that is generally ten years; for non-CDL drivers, three. Verifying less than what the application captures leaves visible unverified entries in the file. What if a non-DOT employer refuses to release anything? Document the refusal with date, contact name, and stated reason. A documented refusal is a complete record. Many small employers have blanket no-verification policies, and that fact belongs in the file rather than being retried indefinitely. Can we accept W-2s or pay stubs instead of employer contact? Applicant-supplied documents can support a verification but shouldn't replace independent employer contact, because they share the same weakness as an applicant-supplied phone number. Where they're the only available evidence, note that explicitly. Does the 30-day response window apply to non-DOT employers? No. The 30-day obligation in §391.23 binds DOT-regulated previous employers responding to a safety performance history request. A non-DOT employer has no federal obligation to respond at all, which is why the escalation ladder and good-faith documentation carry more weight on these entries. The Entries No System Will Close for You The DOT compliance stack is genuinely good at the part of a driver's history it was designed for. Clearinghouse queries, PSP reports, and §391.23 request workflows handle regulated employers inside the three-year window efficiently. Everything else on the application — the small employers, the non-transportation jobs, years four through ten, the gaps — is a manual outreach problem, and it will stay one. The question isn't whether to work it. It's whether the work produces a record an auditor can follow. If your team is spending its week on hold with employers that were never going to be in a database, see how Superunit handles outreach-required verification .

title: Should we use AI voiceover in customer-facing videos?
summary: When an AI voiceover belongs in front of a customer, when a human read earns its cost, and how to make generated narration sound natural in any language.
body_text: When does an AI voiceover belong in customer-facing video? In our opinion for most customer-facing videos, an AI voiceover is the right call if it's educational content, with narrow exceptions. The content that teams ship to customers at any volume is mostly instructional. Onboarding walkthroughs, feature explainers, a step-by-step guide to a workflow, a fix for a support ticket that keeps recurring. Such content gets updated, re-cut, and translated, and a human recording turns every one of those changes into a re-booking. A generated voice turns it into a text edit. The exception is videos that carry a relationship, not information. A renewal thank-you to your largest account, a founder's response to an escalation, a message where the point is partly that a specific person took the time, attention, and care needed for the situation. Such videos deserve a real voice. The value there is the human presence, and no voice model replaces it because replacing it isn't the goal. Most worry lands in the wrong place. Teams assume the customer is running a detector, ready to feel deceived the instant they clock a synthetic voice. In practice a customer reacts to whether the narration is clear, correctly paced, and says the product name right. A flat, robotic read on a support video reads as carelessness. A warm, well-paced AI voiceover on the same video reads as a company that ships good material. The tell that damages trust is low quality, not artificiality. Video type Better choice Why Onboarding and feature walkthroughs AI voiceover High volume, frequently updated, often translated. Re-recording every change is the bottleneck. Recurring support and how-to answers AI voiceover Needs to be consistent and fast to produce; a script edit beats a re-record. Multilingual customer education AI voiceover One script, many languages, without hiring a voice actor per market. Renewal or escalation messages to a key account Human read The point is that a named person showed up. Presence is the value. Executive or brand-defining announcements Human read Tone and emphasis carry meaning a script can't fully specify.

title: Introducing DocLang, a markup language for AI
summary: The lead researcher behind IBM’s popular document parser, Docling, explains why generative AI needs its own document standard.
body_text: AI is upending how we live and work, but the data that could really transform how businesses run is often locked away in outdated or proprietary formats. Docling, IBM’s open-source document parser, has helped to make this information more accessible, allowing enterprises to lift new insights from old charts, customer files, and annual reports. With 32 million downloads and 64,000 stars on GitHub, Docling is IBM’s most successful open-source project ever. It’s been integrated into everything from LangChain to Red Hat’s OpenShift, and even IBM’s own Granite family of LLMs . Now, the researchers behind Docling are introducing its complement: DocLang , a sub-language of XML that has the potential to lower latency and inferencing costs by telling an AI model in fewer tokens where things like a headline ends and a chart caption begins. XML stands for Extensible Markup Language , which was designed to store and move data across apps, databases, and web services. In the 1990s, front-end webpages moved to HTML because it was more forgiving of errors than XML, with its strict parsing rules. HTML also had fixed, ready-to-use visual tags making it easier to use. Though HTML became the markup language of the web, XML never really went away. Docling converts unstructured data from various formats (PDF, PPT, XLSX, MP4), into an internal representation that is serialized into DocLang, a constrained dialect of XML. DocLang’s flavor of XML was designed to be more interpretable for an LLM. We recently caught up with Peter Staar, the lead researcher behind Docling, to learn more about DocLang’s back story, its benefits, and what it will take for enterprises and others to adopt it. IBM's Peter Staar, the lead researcher behind Docling, has released its AI-native complement, DocLang. Why is something like DocLang needed? The document formats we use today were designed for different purposes. PDF tells a renderer where to put pixels. DOCX tells a word processor how to lay out a page. Neither were built for a machine that needs to understand the content. When you push these formats through an AI pipeline, reading order becomes ambiguous, tables collapse, figures lose their captions, and metadata disappears. All this happens before the model even sees the content, which caps its accuracy. How is DocLang different? Its only job is machine understanding. It's an open standard — think JSON for data, or HTML for the web — that natively encodes semantics, layout, bounding boxes, and reading order. Instead of trying to recover structure later, we define a representation from the start. We also take the position that a given piece of content should have exactly one encoding. Two systems that read a document correctly should produce byte-identical output. That property — one document, one representation — is something no previous standard guarantees, and it's what makes DocLang trainable and verifiable. A sub-language of XML, DocLang has the potential to lower latency and inferencing costs by telling an AI model precisely how to interpret graphics. Why did you choose XML as the basis for DocLang? We chose XML for its clean semantic-token link. Each semantic token has an explicit opening and closing form — <text> and </text> — and maps directly to a single LLM token. An open tag is one token, the close tag is another. That one-to-one correspondence means the model isn't wasting capacity learning to parse a fuzzy markup dialect. The structure of both the document and the token stream are identical. We cap the syntax vocabulary at about 1,000 tokens and push property semantics into nested elements rather than attributes, precisely to keep that mapping tight and minimize tokens. Where did you get the idea for DocLang? It came out of an observation while working on table recognition. We were training image-to-sequence models to read tables and output them in HTML. It worked, but it was inefficient and the models kept producing syntactically broken HTML. That led to Optimized Table Structure Language (OTSL), which we published in 2023. Our insight was simple but powerful: if you design a minimal, purpose-built vocabulary instead of borrowing HTML, the model gets more accurate. Inference time goes down and the output is always syntactically correct. The representation does the work we'd been asking the model to do. If this works for tables, we thought, why not for a whole page? That became DocTags, and then SmolDocling , a 256-million parameter vision–language model (VLM) that could convert a page with tables, formulas, code, and charts, in one pass and compete with models 27 times larger. Along the way, we learned what not to do. DocTags wasn't XML-compliant or complete — it just couldn't express some document constructs cleanly. DocLang builds on the core idea of a token-efficient, machine-native representation that is also XML-compliant, complete, and canonical. What are the benefits? A few, and they compound. I’m going to list them out: Higher accuracy with smaller models. The representation does more of the work, as we saw with OTSL and SmolDocling. No hallucinated structure. DocLang’s grammar makes invalid output unrepresentable, be it a non-rectangular table or unclosed element. Whole classes of errors simply can't occur. Lossless and grounded. Full table grids, figure positions, reading order, and bounding boxes are all preserved for the model to process. Consistency you can build on. One canonical encoding per document means you can train on it, diff it, cache it, and verify it. It’s a format you can trust. Governance built in. Things like personally identifiable information flags, RAG permissions, and training constraints live in the document head, not in fragile sidecar files, so compliance metadata stays with the content. It's not just for documents. DocLang’s primitives extend to audio transcripts, images, and video segments, which matters as pipelines go multimodal. Open, with no lock-in. It's an open standard under the governance of the Linux Foundation , so it can be implemented or consumed with any tool or pipeline. What are the challenges ahead? A format is only as valuable as the ecosystem that adopts it. A spec with no implementations is just a document. Adoption will make or break DocLang, which is why we launched it with real support. A second challenge is balancing completeness and consistency. The world of documents is endlessly messy, and each time you add expressiveness to cover an edge case, you risk creating a new way to represent something. Holding the line on "one document, one representation" while still covering real-world complexity is hard, ongoing design work. It's why we're still at version 0.x and treating minor versions as potentially breaking. We'd rather get the canonical form right than freeze it prematurely. Migration cost is a third challenge. Anyone with an existing pipeline has to invest in tooling and retraining to convert. We think the accuracy gains pay for it, but it's a real cost we shouldn't wave away. We also face governance risk in keeping the standard genuinely open and not letting it fragment into vendor-specific versions. That's a people-and-process problem as much as a technical one. What will it take for DocLang to be widely adopted? Standards win when they're easy to adopt and obviously better, not when they're mandated. So, our strategy has three parts. First, you make it free, open, and neutrally governed. DocLang is an open spec under foundation governance with multiple organizations behind it. No vendor lock-in. That's the price of entry for anyone to trust a format with their documents. Then you meet people where they are. This is the most important lever. We're not asking the world to rewrite its pipelines from scratch — we're making DocLang a native output of tools people already use. Docling and ABBYY's FineReader Engine, a software development kit for optical character recognition, can already emit DocLang. The moment your existing parser can produce the standard format, adoption stops being a migration project. You also have to relentlessly prove your case. OTSL and SmolDocling showed that a better representation isn't a matter of aesthetics, it directly improves model accuracy and cuts cost. Developers adopt formats that make their systems measurably better. We lead with that evidence. With enough independent implementations, DocLang becomes the default. It’s the thing your parser emits and your model consumes. Nobody decides to use JSON, they just do. Will DocLang eventually make Docling obsolete? Not at all. They complement each other. Docling is a tool that turns messy real-world files into structured output. DocLang is a standardized format for expressing that output. If anything, DocLang makes Docling more valuable, because now Docling's output is an open standard that any downstream system can consume and that other tools can produce. The whole point of a standard is that no single tool owns it. A document converter and the format it targets aren't in competition any more than a compiler and machine code spec are.

title: MDA SPACE OPENS MDA CHORUS™ CONTROL CENTRE IN QUÉBEC
summary: MONTRÉAL, QC (August 11th, 2026) — MDA Space Ltd. (TSX:MDA; NYSE:MDA), a trusted mission partner to the global defence and space industry, today officially
body_text: New control centre marks a major milestone in operational readiness as momentum builds for constellation’s launch in late 2026 MONTRÉAL, QC (August 11th, 2026) — MDA Space Ltd. (TSX:MDA; NYSE:MDA), a trusted mission partner to the global defence and space industry, today officially opened the MDA CHORUS™ Control Centre in St-Bruno-de-Montarville, Québec, on the south shore of Montreal. The new control centre will serve as the operational hub for MDA CHORUS™ satellite operations, marking a significant step towards operational readiness ahead of the late 2026 launch. Designed to serve commercial and government customers globally, MDA CHORUS™ is a next-generation Earth observation constellation designed and built by MDA Space. Set to provide among the most extensive dual-band synthetic aperture radar imaging capacity available on the market, once commissioned, the constellation will deliver industry-leading 700 km-wide imaging swath and sub-metre high-resolution spotlight images, day or night, regardless of weather conditions. The dual-band satellite constellation enables tipping and cueing, where the leading wide-area C-band satellite images a broad area of interest, and the trailing high-resolution X-band satellite zooms in for a closer look, delivering both broad situational awareness and precise detail in a single pass. “The opening of this new state-of-the-art control centre is a critical and exciting step as we prepare to launch and operationalize MDA CHORUS™," said Mike Greenley, CEO of MDA Space. "Backed by decades of on-orbit operations experience across a team that has supported one of the world’s most important Earth observation space assets and missions, this facility brings together the people, systems and infrastructure required to deliver the extraordinary insights and intelligence that global customers depend on." The MDA CHORUS™ Control Centre consolidates satellite mission operations expertise, bringing together the teams and systems that will manage MDA CHORUS™ in a purpose-built control environment. The facility is equipped to support the full scope of satellite operations, from command and control to mission assurance and Earth observation data delivery. With the MDA CHORUS™ Control Centre now open, MDA Space remains on track for the launch of MDA CHORUS™ in late 2026 and the commencement of commercial operations in early 2027. title: How to Run a Paid POC Through a Marketplace
summary: How to structure a paid proof of concept through AWS Marketplace: private offer shapes, term lengths, conversion paths, and the mistakes that lose deals.
body_text: A paid POC — proof of concept — is a short, priced engagement where the buyer evaluates your product for real money rather than for free. Running it through a cloud marketplace puts that money on their existing cloud bill, which means it draws down committed spend and travels a procurement path their organisation has already approved. The free pilot has a structural problem: nothing that costs nothing is anybody’s priority. Champions who have not spent money have not spent political capital either, and the evaluation drifts until someone reorganises. A paid POC fixes the incentive and creates a second problem — now there is a purchase, which means procurement, which means six weeks. Transacting it through a marketplace is how teams get the first without the second. Here is how to structure one, and where they go wrong. Why run a POC through a marketplace at all? Because the money comes from a budget the buyer has already committed, through a vendor they have already approved. Three things follow from that: It draws down committed spend. Enterprise buyers with a committed cloud agreement have money they must spend with that provider. A marketplace purchase counts against it. That converts your invoice from new spend — which needs a budget owner and an approval — into the consumption of a commitment that already exists. The vendor onboarding is already done. Your buyer’s procurement team has an approved relationship with their cloud provider. The marketplace transaction runs through it, so the vendor-onboarding step that normally precedes a first purchase does not repeat. Conversion does not need re-papering. This is the underrated one. A POC that converts to a full agreement on the same marketplace is an amendment or a new private offer, not a new vendor relationship. The path from pilot to production is a document, not a project. The shapes a paid POC can take A short-term private offer The most common and usually the right answer. A private offer with a term matched to the evaluation, at a price that reflects a pilot rather than a production deployment. AWS supports SaaS contracts where buyers “are either billed in advance for the use of your software, or you can offer them a flexible payment schedule,” and lets customers “pay for additional usage above their contract.” A pilot is exactly the case where a flexible schedule earns its complexity: a small payment to start, the balance on conversion. Private offers also unlock currencies the public listing does not. AWS public listings use US dollars; private offers support USD, EUR, GBP, AUD, JPY, and INR for sellers in India. For an international pilot that detail can remove a whole finance objection. A contract with a deliberately short term Where your product is contract-priced, a short contract term is simpler than a bespoke pilot construct. On Microsoft, one-month contract durations exist with one-time upfront billing, and flexible schedules are available on longer terms “with a private offer only.” One Microsoft rule to know before you promise a term: the desired contract duration must be available on the public plan for it to be eligible as part of a private offer. If your public plans only offer annual, you cannot quietly do a one-month private offer without changing the public plan first. A free trial that converts to a paid pilot Where the technical evaluation is genuinely short and the commercial one is not. AWS notes that all SaaS pricing models support free trials. The risk is the one every PLG team knows: a trial that ends without a decision point produces no urgency at all. Free trials on cloud marketplaces covers designing the expiry properly. A funded POC The cloud providers run partner funding programs that can support proof-of-concept work, with eligibility rules that depend on deal stage and program. Amounts and criteria change, so confirm the current terms with your partner manager rather than working from any published figure — AWS partner funding programs covers what each program is for and where to check. The four things to settle before you send the offer 1. What “success” means, in writing. A POC without written success criteria does not end; it fades. Two or three specific, checkable outcomes, agreed with the champion before the offer goes out. If they cannot be checked in the term you have chosen, the term is wrong. 2. The term, and what happens on the last day. Does access stop? Does it convert automatically? Does it lapse into a monthly arrangement? Decide, and tell the buyer. An entitlement that ends without anyone deciding is how a customer loses access mid-evaluation and blames the product. 3. The conversion mechanism, before you need it. The whole advantage of a marketplace POC is that conversion is a document. Know in advance whether it is an amendment to the existing agreement or a fresh private offer, who issues it, and how long acceptance takes. What buyers see when you send a private offer covers the acceptance flow from their side. 4. Who at the buyer accepts. Marketplace offers are accepted by whoever holds the right permissions on the cloud account, which is frequently not your champion. Identify that person during the POC, not on the day you need a signature. Where paid POCs go wrong Pricing the pilot like a small production deal. The point is to remove friction, and a pilot price that requires an approval chain has removed none. Price it to be approvable by your champion’s own authority where you can. A term shorter than the buyer’s own process. A 30-day POC inside an organisation that reviews security in six weeks is a POC that expires during the security review. Match the term to their calendar, not to your quarter. Treating the POC as the sale. The POC is a step, and the conversion offer should be drafted before the pilot ends, not after the results arrive. Momentum decays fast at the end of a pilot. Letting it convert silently. A pilot that auto-converts into a production agreement nobody discussed produces exactly one outcome: a refund conversation and a damaged relationship. Convert deliberately. Forgetting the entitlement ends. When a POC entitlement expires, your product should react. If it does not, you have a customer using production software with no contract behind them, and nothing in your reporting will say so. Frequently asked questions What is a paid POC on AWS Marketplace? A short, priced proof-of-concept engagement transacted through the marketplace, usually as a private offer with a term matched to the evaluation. The cost lands on the buyer’s existing cloud bill. Why run a proof of concept through a marketplace? It draws down the buyer’s committed cloud spend, reuses a vendor relationship procurement has already approved, and lets a successful pilot convert without a new vendor onboarding. How long should a marketplace POC run? Long enough to complete the buyer’s own security and evaluation processes. A term shorter than their internal review guarantees an expiry mid-evaluation. Can I offer a one-month term on Microsoft Marketplace? Yes, one-month contract durations exist with one-time upfront billing. Note that a duration must be available on your public plan before it is eligible as part of a private offer. Can a POC be billed in instalments? On AWS, yes. SaaS contracts can be billed in advance or on a flexible payment schedule, so a pilot can start with a small payment and settle the balance on conversion. What should happen when a POC ends? Whatever you told the buyer would happen. Decide in advance whether access stops, converts or lapses — and make sure your product actually reacts when the entitlement ends. Takeaways A paid POC on a marketplace draws down committed cloud spend and reuses an approved procurement path, which is why it moves faster than a direct pilot. The usual instrument is a short-term private offer. AWS supports billing in advance or on a flexible payment schedule, plus overage above the contract. Private offers also open currencies the public listing does not — AWS supports USD, EUR, GBP, AUD, JPY and INR on private offers. On Microsoft, a contract duration must exist on the public plan before it can be used in a private offer. Write down success criteria and the end-of-term behaviour before sending the offer. A POC without either does not end, it fades. Draft the conversion offer before the pilot finishes. Momentum at the end of a pilot decays in days. A pilot is only fast if the offer, the conversion and the entitlement behind them are one continuous record. See how Suger handles private offers — pilot terms, flexible schedules and the conversion offer that follows — across every marketplace you sell on.

title: How Ambient AI Scribes Can Boost Patient Satisfaction in Specialty Practices by 2025
summary: By 2025, specialty practices are using ambient AI scribes to dramatically improve patient satisfaction by cutting screen time, boosting face-to-face interaction, and delivering real-time, patient-friendly summaries. These tools help providers spend up to 85% of visits focused on patients, raising “felt heard” scores, reducing post-visit calls, and strengthening overall trust and engagement.
body_text: Patients notice when you’re really listening. In a 2024 Press Ganey survey, 68% of specialty patients said the #1 driver of a 5-star visit was “My doctor gave me their full attention.” Yet most providers spend 40–50% of the encounter typing. Enter ambient AI scribes—the quiet tech that’s flipping the script. By 2025, mid-market ortho, cardio, and derm groups are using AI to cut screen time, boost face-to-face moments, and lift patient satisfaction scores without adding staff or chaos. Here’s how it works—and the proof it’s moving the needle. The Hidden Link: Less Typing = Happier Patients The old way with human charting and EHRs meant providers kept their eyes on the screen for 60% of the visit, finished notes 4–6 hours later, and left patients feeling rushed. The new way with ambient AI shifts eyes to the patient for 85% or more of the visit, delivers a draft note in under 10 seconds, and makes patients feel truly heard. 3 Ways Ambient AI Scribes Raise Patient Satisfaction More Eye Contact, Less “Computer Talk” AI listens passively with no extra device in the patient’s face. Providers maintain natural posture and tone. The result is HCAHPS “communication” scores rising 14–18 points in pilot clinics. Faster, Friendlier Discharge AI generates patient-friendly summaries alongside clinical notes. Hand the patient a printed or texted plain-language recap with clear instructions like “Avoid stairs for 2 weeks,” “Take meds with food,” or “Follow-up in 6 weeks.” Practices report 28% fewer post-visit calls. Shorter Wait-for-Answers Time Notes close in real-time, portals update faster, and patients see results the same day. One cardiology group cut “result wait” complaints by 41%. By-the-Numbers Impact (Mid-Market Benchmarks) From internal Athelas timing studies in 2025, provider face-time jumped from 42% to 88%. Press Ganey pulse surveys showed “felt heard” ratings climbing from 76% to 93%. EHR audit logs revealed portal result delays dropping from 3.2 days to 0.4 days. Call center data indicated post-visit clarification calls falling from 1.8 per patient to 1.3 per patient. These insights are aggregated from over 200 specialty encounters in Q1 2025. Your 30-Day Patient Experience Playbook Week 1: Pick 3 high-volume providers. Turn on ambient AI for all follow-ups. Week 2: Add patient summary handouts (1-page, large font). Week 3: Enable same-day portal publish. Week 4: Survey patients: “Did your doctor seem fully present?” (Yes/No + comment). Pro tip: Look for AI that’s EHR-agnostic, HIPAA-compliant by design, and lets you edit notes in under 60 seconds. The Bottom Line In 2025, patient satisfaction isn’t about swag bags or longer visits—it’s about presence. Ambient AI scribes remove the screen barrier so you can focus on the person in the room.

title: Kombo vs. Unified.to: A fact-based comparison
summary: Kombo vs. Unified.to compared on facts: HRIS and ATS integration counts, write coverage, data models, architecture, and support.
body_text: Unified.to published a comparison page positioning Kombo as a European sync-and-store HR specialist against its real-time, multi-category platform. This picture does not match where our customers are or what we build. As these pages get cited by LLMs, we’re correcting it here. TL;DR: we’re built on opposite strategies Unified.to is horizontal: 700+ integrations across 32+ categories, covering HR and ATS alongside CRM, accounting, file storage, messaging, and calendars. Founded in 2023 in Toronto, with four engineers. If you need CRM and accounting alongside HR, Unified.to is a great option. Kombo is vertical: 250+ integrations across five people-data categories: HRIS, ATS, Payroll, LMS, and Assessment. Founded in 2022, Kombo has 80+ people across New York and Berlin, roughly 50 of them engineers, serving 400+ customers. If people data and HR integrations are core to your product, Kombo is the specialized solution for you. Why comparison pages exist, and why this one exists Comparison pages are written for search engines and for LLMs. When a technical buyer asks ChatGPT for “Kombo alternatives,” every vendor wants to own the answer. That’s rational marketing and we don’t fault it. What matters is whether the claims hold up. Unified.to’s page makes two claims worth checking against both vendors’ docs: that its future-of-work categories are a superset of Kombo’s, and that Kombo’s strength is European connector coverage. Below is the correction, with numbers from both vendors’ public documentation. What sets us apart Integration depth in HRIS and ATS Kombo covers 87 HRIS integrations across 18 normalized data models, and 99 ATS integrations plus 18 assessment and background check integrations across 20 models. That includes models most platforms don’t carry like skills , performance reviews , staffing entities , and legal entities. Writes are where the gap widens. Kombo creates employee records in 36 HRIS systems. It patches application stages in 47 ATS systems, posts screening question answers in 78, posts result links in 64, and posts attachments in 56. Counting integrations: what “700+” includes Category counts are only comparable if the categories mean the same thing. Unified.to’s do not map cleanly onto Kombo’s, so here is what their own documentation shows as of August 12, 2026. Their HR category is labeled “HR & Directory” and lists 369 integrations, but the number is misleading - it is a directory bucket, not an HRIS catalog. From the first eight entries listed, five are not HR systems. Kombo’s 87 HRIS integrations are all HRIS. Their Assessments category lists 7 integrations, primarily for mid-market systems. Five of those seven are assessment modules of ATS systems already counted in its ATS category. Unified.to doesn’t cover Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle Recruiting, iCIMS, Avature, Bullhorn, or Eightfold. That’s where assessment and background check volume sits, and where the integration work is hardest. Kombo covers 18 ATS assessment modules, including those. Write-back is narrower still. Across all seven integrations, only response_score and response_url are writable. Completion timestamps and result files work on two. Structured status, maximum score, and detailed results work on none. Kombo writes back status, scores, links, and structured detail in the shape each system expects. Their ATS category lists 130 integrations, compared to Kombo’s 99, so in terms of system count they cover more. The model is nine objects: activity, application, application status, candidate, company, document, interview, job, scorecard. There is no offer, no rejection reason, no screening question, no tag or source. Kombo runs 20 normalized models across ATS and assessment, and publishes how many systems support each write. Enterprise readiness for Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle HCM, and UKG Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle HCM, and UKG are closed ecosystems. Access depends on vendor partnerships, and behavior differs across tenants and versions. Listing the connector is the easy part. Kombo holds partnership-level access and sandbox environments for all four. Those took years to negotiate. Initial syncs of large instances are monitored by Kombo engineers, because a 40,000-employee Workday tenant will hit rate limits on first pull and the failure mode is partial data, not an error. We have not seen evidence that Unified.to holds equivalent partnerships or sandboxes for these systems, and its own page positions white-glove onboarding for SAP SuccessFactors and Workday as a Kombo strength rather than a shared one. If you sell to enterprises running these systems, ask for sandbox access during the trial. The answer is diagnostic. Reliability, and who is behind the integration when it breaks Unified.to has four engineers maintaining a catalog of 700+ integrations across 32+ categories - more than 175 integrations per engineer. Kombo has roughly 50 engineers on 250 integrations in five categories, roughly five per engineer. We’re not claiming their integrations don’t work. We are saying that maintenance load in this category is relentless and mostly invisible. HRIS vendors ship breaking changes without notice, deprecate fields mid-quarter, and enforce rate limits that differ per tenant. Every integration you list is a standing maintenance commitment, and that commitment does not shrink when you add a category. Kombo runs six dedicated support engineers plus a rotation of three to five product engineers, roughly 10% of the company at any time. Every customer on every plan gets a Slack channel with the engineers who built their integrations. Support runs from New York and Berlin, so US and EU business hours are covered by people who have already debugged the system you’re stuck on. The architecture argument, taken seriously Unified.to’s central claim is that pass-through is the next generation and sync-and-store is the previous one. The argument is coherent and worth answering directly because, for people data, the trade-off runs the other way. Most HRIS and ATS systems do not offer usable webhooks. They offer paginated REST endpoints with tight, tenant-specific rate limits. If you read live on every request, those limits become your product’s problem. Kombo absorbs them: we sync on a schedule, default every three hours and configurable to every minute on higher plans, forward real-time change webhooks where the source supports them, and expose forced syncs when you need current state now. That’s what makes high-volume, real-time AI workloads economical. An agent screening candidates or reconciling headcount reads the same records hundreds of times and reads unpredictably. On a metered pass-through model, every read is a billable call against a rate limit you don’t control, so your bill and your failure rate both scale with how hard your model thinks. On Kombo, reads hit a normalized copy with unlimited calls inside each connection and no upstream throttling in your agent’s path. A stored copy also gives you things a live read cannot. Deletion tracking, because a record vanishing from a paginated response is ambiguous until you reconcile. Change history, so you can tell what moved. Continuity when the upstream system has an outage, which for HR systems is a regular Tuesday. On the “Kombo is the EU specialist” framing A central claim made by Unified.to is that Kombo is a specialized player for European systems. This likely comes as a surprise to all the leading US scale-ups and enterprises building on us, such as Indeed, Greenhouse, Wellhub, Juicebox, HireVue, KarmaCheck, Alex.ai, and Thatch. To set the record straight, Kombo is a global integration infrastructure provider with offices in New York and Berlin. More than half of Kombo’s revenue comes from the United States, and it covers the most HRIS and ATS integrations in the US market among all unified APIs, including Workday, UKG, Oracle HCM, BambooHR, Gusto, Namely, Lattice, Remote, Greenhouse, and Lever. Our support engineers work from New York and Berlin, so a US buyer’s escalation is handled within their own business day and jurisdiction (a clause that appears in most US enterprise DPAs). The EU framing is smart positioning. Kombo does carry deep coverage of Personio, PayFit, Factorial, Softgarden, AFAS, Cegid, and d.vinci, and no horizontal platform matches it there. Painting that depth as the boundary of our market, rather than as one part of it, turns a strength into a limitation. It reads well on a comparison page, but does not describe the company. Correcting the comparison table Figures from both vendors’ public documentation and public company data, as of August 12, 2026. Feature comparison Kombo Unified.to Focus and scale Categories 5 (HRIS, ATS, Payroll, LMS, Assessment) 32+, including HR plus CRM, accounting, messaging, file storage Total integrations 250+ 700+ Engineers ~50 4 Integrations per engineer ~5 175+ Founded 2022 (Y Combinator) 2023 (Techstars) Offices New York and Berlin Toronto Customers 400+ Not published HRIS capabilities Dedicated HRIS integrations 87 369 listed officially, but most are not HR systems Normalized HRIS data models 18 14 Skills data model ✅ ❌ Performance data model ✅ ❌ Staffing entities data model ✅ ❌ Legal entity and location models ✅ ❌ Benefits, bank account, deduction models Roadmap Q4 2026 11 integrations Creating employee records 36 integrations ❌ Getting absences 34 integrations 49 integrations ATS capabilities API-based ATS integrations 99 130 Normalized models across ATS and assessment 20 9 Offer object ✅ ❌ Screening question object ✅ ❌ Rejection reason object ✅ ❌ Posting applications All integrations 55 integrations Patch application stage 47 integrations 31 integrations Posting screening question answers 78 integrations 19 integrations Posting result link to application 64 and background check Dedicated assessment integrations 18 7 Assessment data objects 4 2 Background check module ✅ ❌ Ordering assessments ✅ ✅ Returning results and scores to the ATS ✅ Partially (no status, maximum score, or subscores) Enterprise readiness Partnerships with Workday, SAP SF, Oracle HCM, UKG ✅ with sandbox access ❌ Built-in sandboxes ✅ all plans ❌ Large-instance sync monitoring (10,000+ employees) ✅ engineer-monitored Not documented Rate-limit handling for slow source fields Managed by Kombo Handled in your retry logic Deletion tracking ✅ ❌ Resilience during upstream outage ✅ serves last known state ❌ ISO 27001 ✅ ❌ SOC 2 Type II ✅ ✅ HIPAA ✅ ✅ GDPR ✅ ✅ Data residency US and EU US, EU, AU Support/engineering personnel location US and EU Canada Support Dedicated Slack channel All plans ❌ Support in US business hours ✅ New York office ✅ Toronto office Dedicated support engineers 6 plus 3 to 5 rotating product engineers ❌ Implementation support Scale and Enterprise ❌ What we hear from teams migrating off Unified.to The following comes from a US enterprise SaaS company that ran Unified.to in production before moving to Kombo. Quotes are from recorded evaluation calls in May and June 2026, lightly redacted for better readability. Their engineering lead on the mechanics: We have a certain field that’s slow, and then we’re getting a 420 rate limiting error, and we’ve been doing a lot of exponential retry backup [sic] to solve these issues. On the same call, they were running manual delta and full syncs on a three hour cycle, and building their own retry and backoff layer around a live pass-through read. Their VP then explained further on why the rollout with Unified.to stalled: Quite frankly, we’ve been slow rolling out with our customers because we haven’t been confident in Unified. We started with two small customers, and we ended up building the integration ourselves. Another enterprise customer got stalled because we were not ... confident onboarding them with Unified. It just hasn’t been efficient or reliable. On trust and testing: I can’t really trust what’s been built. I’ve seen some of the, like, reliability challenges, right, and, and lack of sandbox, right? And so it’s been a big concern for us. While this is arguably just one customer, the failure pattern directly stems from their pass-through and platform architecture: rate limits surfacing as your problem, no sandbox to reproduce them in, and an enterprise rollout that stops because nobody wants to bet a named account on it. When Unified.to is the better choice You need HR integrations, as well as other categories like CRM or accounting. Kombo does not cover those categories and will not. If your security narrative to customers is that no third party persists their data, then Unified.to’s architecture is the better choice. You prefer self-serve entry pricing - $750 a month, including a trial, is a great offering. Kombo cannot offer this, as we must first scope the use case and related requirements (expected data volume, customer complexity, sync frequency, etc.) before providing a quote. When Kombo is the better choice Your product is HR tech, talent, benefits, payroll, or AI workforce tooling, and people data is the core of your product. Your customers run Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle HCM, or UKG, and you need partnership access and sandboxes - pass-through architectures tend to strain at that scale. You need deep write coverage, for operations such as creating employees, patching application stages, posting screening answers and attachments across dozens of systems. You sell screening or background checks and need results and scores flowing back into the ATS, not just an assessment order. Your end customers’ security reviews ask where data is accessed from, and require ISO 27001. You need support engineers in your time zone who have already debugged the specific system your customer runs. One last thing Pressure-test both platforms on the systems and operations your product actually needs, not on category counts. Ask both of us: How many engineers work on my category, and how many integrations does each maintain? Which specific systems support the writes I need, and can you show me the per-system list? Do you have a sandbox for Workday and SAP SuccessFactors, and can I have access this week? What happens on the first sync of a 40,000-employee tenant, and who watches it? When a source field is slow and starts throttling, whose code handles the backoff? When an HRIS ships a breaking change on a Friday, who notices and how fast? What share of your roadmap next year goes into HRIS and ATS? Those answers will tell you more than any comparison page. Unified.to is building something genuinely hard, and the horizontal bet is a legitimate one. We just think people data rewards the opposite bet. Frequently asked questions Is Kombo a European unified API? + No. Kombo is a global unified API for people data with offices in New York and Berlin. More than half of Kombo’s revenue comes from the United States, US customers include Indeed, Greenhouse, Experian, and Gem, and Kombo offers both US and EU data residency. Deep European HRIS coverage is one part of the catalog, not its boundary. How is Kombo different from Unified.to? + Kombo covers five people-data categories across 250+ integrations with roughly 50 engineers. Unified.to covers 32+ categories across 700+ integrations with four engineers. Kombo trades breadth for depth per system, especially in write operations and enterprise HRIS. Which platform is better for assessments and background checks? + Kombo. Unified.to lists 7 assessment integrations, 5 of which are assessment modules of ATS systems already counted in its ATS category, with a two-object model covering order and package. Kombo covers 18 dedicated assessment and background check integrations, returns results and scores to the ATS, includes a background check module, and auto-answers screening questions. Does Unified.to cover the same HRIS and ATS systems as Kombo? + It covers the same categories and a large overlap of systems, but the difference lies in depth per system: documented write operations, normalized models for skills, performance, and staffing entities, and partnership-level access with sandboxes for Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle HCM, and UKG. Is pass-through better than sync-and-store for HR data? + It depends on the source systems. Most HRIS and ATS platforms lack usable webhooks and enforce tenant-specific rate limits, so live reads push throttling and retry logic into your application. A managed sync layer absorbs that and adds deletion tracking, change history, and continuity during upstream outages. Notably, Unified.to ships Database Sync so customers can store records themselves for high-volume reads. How reliable are integrations maintained by a small team? + Maintenance load scales with the number of integrations, not the size of the team. HRIS vendors ship breaking changes without notice and enforce per-tenant rate limits, so each listed integration is an ongoing commitment. A catalog of 700+ integrations maintained by four engineers carries structurally more risk per integration than 250 maintained by 50. How hard is it to migrate from Unified.to to Kombo? + Straightforward in most cases, since you’re replacing one unified API with another. The main change is that scheduled syncs, rate-limit handling, and retry logic move from your codebase to Kombo’s. Kombo provides sandboxes to validate every data flow before go-live, and support engineers map existing flows during onboarding.

title: 10 Easy Porch Ideas to Upgrade Your Space
summary: Get inspiration to refresh your porch or start decorating here. Whether it's screened, your front porch, back porch, or small, get easy porch ideas here.
body_text: Free image via Unsplash When it comes to the overall impact your home has, your front porch packs a big punch. If you enjoy entertaining guests or simply spending time outdoors, your back porch deserves just as much attention. Yet many don’t know what to do with this space, leaving the porch, screened in or not, bare and neglected. Even worse, this leaves us without the option to enjoy it. While the origins of the porch as an architectural feature are a topic of debate among scholars (some believe they were invented during the Greek and Roman empires while others believe they got their beginnings in Equatorial Africa), the benefits are clear. They help us commune with nature, connect with our communities, and take in the world around us rather than the one within our four walls. They can also provide relief on nights when the outdoors is cooler than the indoors (which anyone who’s slept on a screened-in porch can tell you). So, if you have a porch but aren’t quite sure how to put it to its best use – you’re in the right spot. We have easy porch upgrades you can do today to get the most you can out of your exterior spaces, including guidance on how to style your space and pick the right décor for your porch. And even if your “porch” is more of a landing or back patio than a traditional porch, these tips apply just the same. It’s all about making what you’ve got work better for you and your lifestyle. Clean Your Space A bright, welcoming, and clean porch starts with a plan. Follow these steps for cleaning a porch to prep, clean, and protect your space so it stays inviting all season. Think of it as cleaning your porch to refresh the space from top to bottom. Declutter Your Porch Donate or sell furniture and décor you no longer want Only keep existing pieces that fit your space and style Remove everything from your porch while you clean Clean Surfaces, Furniture, and Décor Start by clearing leaves and old plants from your porch Sweep and remove all dirt or mud from floors and walls Clean waterproof furniture like tables, chairs, and rugs with a hose and soap Gently clean smaller décor pieces Identify any spots requiring deep cleans or furniture repairs Protect, Style, and Store After cleaning, put back furniture and décor you’re keeping Anything seasonal you don’t want out, put into storage Consider using a storage unit to hold seasonal items or rotating items Storage lockers are good for small décor, while regular units can hold furniture items like chairs and tables. Choose a Porch Theme & Aesthetic Free image via Unsplash Your porch is clean, but now it’s time to pick a style that matches your vibe and vision. Look at what furniture and décor you already have and the bones of your existing porch to get started. Or start totally fresh and pick something new below. Style ideas for your porch: Thrifted and Colorful Slowly curate furniture and décor only from thrift and secondhand stores Search for colorful pieces with character Mix and match patterns and palettes Green and Floral Focus on decorating with live (or fake) plants Find furniture with natural finishes like wood or wicker Install flower boxes or trellises for greenery Clean and Calm Pick furniture that is comfortable and perfect for lounging Find neutral colors and simple patterns to keep things calm Match your colors, décor, and finish with your porch’s existing vibe to stay cohesive Porch Décor Ideas Now that you’ve picked your aesthetic, let’s dive into what you can change right now on your porch, whether you have a blank space or existing décor to work with. Porch Furniture No matter your best intentions, you’re just not going to hang out on your porch unless you have comfortable furniture, so plan to spend a little time – and maybe even a little cash – on this one. The good news is that even some interior furniture can last a long time on a porch, so you do have some flexibility. Try to be creative and scour Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and secondhand shops for castaways. Porch furniture that can refresh your space should be: Chairs, for dining or lounging Tables, either dining or end tables Swinging chairs (if you can safely hang them) Functional storage like ottomans or chests When picking porch furniture, make sure it’s: Easy to clean Matches your aesthetic / theme Comfortable enough that you’ll use it repeatedly Potted Plants and Flowers It’s amazing what a beautifully potted plant can do to an environment. Make sure that the ones you pick are well-suited for the shade or sun that your porch gets and put them in pots that drain well and match the other elements on the porch. A cute look is old crockery tubs or other antique ceramics on the steps. Plant ideas for your porch: Planter boxes for your railing Hanging plants that drape Potted plants to put on the ground or on stands Climbing plants on a trellis for privacy Rugs and Mats There are many exterior rugs on the market now that are made from durable materials designed for outdoor use and are great at hiding a multitude of problems with your floors. Interior and exterior. These pieces can add a real flair to a porch, especially when they have bright, bold colors and patterns. Rugs and mats good for porches: Welcome mats with seasonal or fun sayings Rubber mats for holding dirty shoes or yard supplies Large outdoor area rugs to cover sun damaged porch floors Accent outdoor rugs in bold styles to add color Seasonal Décor Free image via Unsplash Seasonal décor is a great way to decorate your porch, but it looks the best when you switch it out for the right seasons. Check out our easy seasonal décor recommendations below, but don’t forget to make a plan for how you’ll store your seasonal décor that’s not in use. Easy seasonal décor for your porch: A faux wreath for every season Reusable faux florals that match (and will survive) the weather Holiday specific figurines and table décor Flags for your favorite sports teams Lighting and Warmth Lights are key to a great porch experience. Use lights to set the vibe you want; you’ll be surprised how different it can be based on what you choose. This includes lighting from an actual flame (if it’s safe and legal in your area) like outdoor fireplaces. Porch lighting options to brighten your space: String up some Edison bulbs or holiday lights for a classic look Plug in a more traditional statement lamp to bring the living room out Hanging or floor lanterns add vertical interest Candles flickering in hurricane glasses are warm and welcoming Shade and Cover Equally important to light is shade. A porch isn’t fit for relaxing without it, so if it doesn’t come your way naturally, you should hang a strategically placed curtain, sun sail or awning to create your own shade. Taking any of those steps will dramatically increase porch usage and enjoyment, but if you really want to get fancy – you could even add some misters to cool down in the summer months. Easy ways to shade your porch: Umbrellas if your porch is uncovered Trellises with plants or other coverings Curtains that double as privacy in busy neighborhoods Retractable (or permanent) awning covers Door Décor A dinged door can take away a lot of curb appeal, while a nice fresh layer of paint or two can really amp up the value. Bonus points if you use a fresh new color like hot pink or bright yellow. Glossy hardware in whatever the “metal of the moment” is can also be a relatively cheap and quick way to make an old door do new tricks. Ways to spruce up your front door: Add a seasonal wreath Paint it a bold accent color Include a unique door knocker for function and style While we think the above tips are applicable to any porch, we know that depending on the size and location of your porch, it can be tough to know where to start. Below are our summarized (and new!) tips for decorating your porch depending on its size and location. Front Porch Ideas Free image via Unsplash Create cohesive curb appeal with coordinated colors and durable materials that stand up to the elements. Choose a weatherproof rug to anchor the seating area. Pair a bench or rocking chairs with fade-resistant cushions. Flank the door with matching planters or wall sconces for symmetry. Keep clutter contained in a lidded storage bench. Use dusk-to-dawn lighting for safety and a welcoming glow. Swap wreaths, doormats, and pillows seasonally to keep the front porch fresh year-round. Back Porch Ideas Transform the back porch into a flexible retreat by defining zones and layering comfort. Designate a dining zone with a weather-resistant table and chairs. Create a conversation area with an outdoor sofa, chairs, and a low table. Layer ambience using string lights, lanterns, and a dimmable pendant. Add outdoor curtains or lattice screens for privacy and shade. Install a ceiling fan or portable fans to improve airflow on hot days. Incorporate a bar cart or storage cabinet for grilling tools and games. Small Porch Ideas Make every inch count with compact, multifunctional pieces and vertical accents. Choose foldable chairs, a bistro set, or a single lounge chair to save space. Use a slim side table that doubles as a plant stand or extra seating. Go vertical with railing planters, wall-mounted shelves, and hanging baskets. Brighten the area with light-colored rugs. Keep décor minimal to maintain clear pathways and a tidy look. Use for multi-use storage like a cube ottoman or storage stool. Select collapsible or stackable pieces for easy rearranging and storage. Unify your home’s outdoor look by echoing colors and materials across front, back, and small porches. If your space is even smaller, check out our ideas to decorate your small outdoor patio for even more inspiration. Porch Storage to Keep Your Space Clear If you’ve gone through these steps and your space still feels cluttered, storage units are a great way to store furniture and décor of any kind, either indoor or outdoor. Consider using a storage unit while completing porch renovation projects, so your items stay out of the elements, or even while you’re in the design phase. Find a CubeSmart storage facility near you to get started.
